content: Levonorgestrel is an oral emergency contraceptive approved by the FDA for preventing pregnancy after unprotected sexual intercourse or suspected contraceptive failure. It is most effective when taken as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of the event. The standard dosage is a single oral tablet containing 1.5 mg of levonorgestrel. Common side effects include menstrual irregularities, nausea, lower abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, and dizziness. Levonorgestrel is contraindicated in cases of known or suspected pregnancy, as it is not effective in terminating an existing pregnancy. It is important to consider the possibility of ectopic pregnancy in women who experience severe lower abdominal pain or delayed menstruation after taking the medication. A follow-up physical or pelvic examination is recommended if there is any uncertainty about the patient’s health or pregnancy status. Levonorgestrel does not provide protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). It is not intended for routine contraception, and fertility may return rapidly after use. Women should resume or initiate a regular contraceptive method as soon as possible after taking levonorgestrel. Clinical trials have shown that levonorgestrel prevents approximately 84% of expected pregnancies when taken as directed. The most common adverse events reported in clinical studies include heavier menstrual bleeding (30.9%), nausea (13.7%), lower abdominal pain (13.3%), fatigue (13.3%), and headache (10.3%). Postmarketing reports have also identified side effects such as vomiting, dizziness, dysmenorrhea, irregular menstruation, oligomenorrhea, and pelvic pain. Levonorgestrel’s mechanism of action involves preventing ovulation or fertilization by altering the transport of sperm or ova. It may also inhibit implantation by modifying the endometrium, but it is not effective once implantation has occurred. The drug is metabolized in the liver and excreted primarily in the urine and feces. Certain medications and herbal products, such as barbiturates, rifampin, and St. John’s wort, may reduce the effectiveness of levonorgestrel by inducing enzymes that metabolize progestins. Patients should consult their healthcare provider about potential drug interactions. Levonorgestrel is classified as Pregnancy Category X by the FDA, indicating that it should not be used during pregnancy. However, studies have not shown significant adverse effects on fetal development with long-term use of progestins. Small amounts of levonorgestrel may pass into breast milk, but no significant effects on breastfeeding performance or infant health have been reported. Levonorgestrel is not intended for use in postmenopausal women or premenarchal adolescents. Limited data suggest that its safety and efficacy are similar in postpubertal adolescents and adult women. No specific studies have evaluated the effects of race, renal impairment, or hepatic impairment on the drug’s pharmacokinetics. The medication is supplied as a peach-colored, round tablet embossed with 287 on one side and WATSON on the other. It should be stored at controlled room temperature (20° to 25°C or 68° to 77°F). Patients should be counseled to take the tablet as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse and to seek medical attention if they experience severe abdominal pain or delayed menstruation. If vomiting occurs within two hours of taking the tablet, they should contact their healthcare provider to discuss whether a repeat dose is necessary. Levonorgestrel is marketed under various brand names, including Plan B, Plan B One-Step, Next Choice, My Way, Mirena, and Skyla.
